lines.narration: Arizona, and a boy who cannot sit still. In the auto shop a dark-haired teenager watches three jocks pin a classmate to a roller door and scrawl a mark on his bare stomach, and his jaw sets.
He slides open a tool drawer and lifts out jumper-cable clamps, then turns back toward the fight.

Out in the student lot a blonde girl on a red convertible looks him over. "It's a nice ride." He answers, "It's not the ride, it's the rider" — right as the blond jock in the #13 jersey plants himself beside her. "You talking to my girl?"
The jock trashes the muscle car and brags on his Viper. Our teenager fires back the specs cold — five hundred horsepower, zero to sixty in 4.3. The jock sneers: "You can read the brochure."

claim.subject: the blond jock in the #13 jersey

lines.narration: So the teenager calls it: race for pink slips. The jock flinches. "This car goes for 80 grand. What would I do with a broken-ass piece of shit like that?" He wants the win without the risk.

claim.subject: the blond jock in the #13 jersey

lines.narration: Then the girl settles it herself. Winner gets — "Me." And now there is nothing left to haggle over. The race is on, and she is the trophy.
A half-built housing tract. Jocks crouch at a Shang-Ri-La Estates billboard, an arm drops, and both cars tear away in a wall of dust into the unfinished street.
The girl rides shotgun with the jock, twisting round to watch the chase. They run neck and neck between the framed houses, and the teenager is grinning like this is a gift.
The Viper pulls clear in a dust cloud and leads into the next straight. On pavement the eighty-thousand-dollar car simply has more. He is losing, and he knows it.

claim.subject: the dark-haired teenager in the blue T-shirt

lines.narration: So he quits the road. He yanks the wheel and cuts straight across the raw dirt lots while the Viper stays politely on the pavement — trading grip for a shortcut no sane driver takes.

claim.subject: the dark-haired teenager in the blue T-shirt

lines.narration: He comes back onto blacktop canted up on two wheels, leaning his car bodily against the convertible, smirking across the gap. The girl half-smiles at him. The jock stares dead ahead, jaw set, and there is the mistake.

claim.subject: the dark-haired teenager in the cream muscle car

lines.narration: The two cars touch at speed. The muscle car launches off the dirt and tumbles end over end as the spectators scatter.
It settles upside down, wheels still turning, and there he hangs in his belt, face smeared with blood — both cars wrecked in front of a crowd full of cameras.

At the station a detective plays him grainy bystander video of the race. "You think this is a joke?" The rich kids out front — Ken and Barbie — walk without a slap on the wrist, their parents too hooked up.

"But I like screw-ups like you," the detective says, "because you're 100% guaranteed conviction." Then: the car's been crushed. The boy comes out of his chair — "You did what?" — and a deputy shoves him back down.
His mother storms in swinging — "What the hell were you thinking?" — then drops into a chair, asks the officer if it's illegal to smoke in here, and starts working the man instead of the boy.

She smokes while the detective lays out the arithmetic. Two priors for reckless driving, willful destruction of property — this makes it strike three. Prison, unless, as she puts it, there's got to be another way.

Out in the corridor he asks the only question that matters to a kid who's done this before: "Where are we moving this time?" His mother looks at him. "We're not moving anywhere." He takes the sentence in silence.
The another way is an ocean. The crew-cut American teenager lands alone in Tokyo, rides an escalator past posters he can't read, and pushes out into the crowd.
An orange taxi carries him across an elevated expressway at dusk, his reflection sliding over the glass — shipped to the far side of the world for refusing to lose one race.
